rv.q: Seven years on, Miriam has become more insistent in her denial that what happened to Oscar may never be known, despite the ominous discovery of his wallet in a public bathroom toilet. She sneers at David’s suggestion that the family hold a memorial as a way of moving on.
Her laserlike focus on finding the truth cuts through an otherwise stilted and overwrought play.
Lauren Ambrose is devastating in this shattering, nonlinear, and theatrical English family drama.
The Unbelievers is a deeply affecting piece about a woman slowly unwinding and a family desperately trying to keep her, and themselves, together. And with Ambrose as the lead, it's unmissable.

Payne's adept writing, which often blurs genre and places tight comedy against deep pathos, and Knud Adams's skillful, confident direction place us inside Miriam's mind, and the result is a stunning piece of theatre likely to stick in your own.
The Unbelievers does boast one crowning achievement: the red-haired Lauren Ambrose.

While The Unbelievers proves unconvincing as a domestic drama, it offers a riveting character study of a woman who responds to an unthinkable situation in the only way she knows how, all others be damned.
a journey that engulfs the audience in a kind of anguish as each unresolved piece is presented and then removed before a true conclusion can be reached

cn.t: Critics are divided on this nonlinear family drama about a missing child, praising Lauren Ambrose's devastating performance and striking set design while faulting its fragmented structure that frustrates more than it illuminates.

vr.q: The Unbelievers had me mostly on the edge of my seat with its compelling premise and even more compelling ensemble work.
